column3: Generic recompense for deeds; no distinct account of mutual restraint.
Contrasts speech with conduct, clarifying the failure of moral words without corresponding action.
Presents sustained worship as a practice that restrains indecency and wrong.
Closest institutional parallel: learned authorities fail to restrain wrongdoing and corrupt gain.
Supplies the opening doctrinal breach in the immediate 5:72-86 sequence.
Directly joins enjoining good, restraining wrong, and endurance in a disciplined response.
Names the ongoing sins and corrupt gain that 5:63 and 5:79 leave unrestrained.
Gives the preceding condemnation for persistent disobedience and transgression.
Shows an imposed stopping point when a wrongdoer will not desist.
Only a generic reference to a people's deeds.
Provides the positive counterpattern of belief and righteous action after the speech-conduct critique.
Shows prohibition used perversely to exclude others while its agents withdraw themselves.
Generic fragmentation and later accounting, without a restraint relation.
Continues the immediate sequence with a warning to desist from wrongful speech.
Generic punitive response, without communal prevention.
Record of deeds only.
Sets the immediate warning against excess and inherited misguidance before the condemnation.
Frames avoidance of prohibited grave wrongs as an individual boundary.
Negative evaluation of allegiance without a restraint relation.
Links failure to desist from destabilizing conduct with an external communal consequence.
Defines reciprocal believer solidarity through enjoining good and restraining wrong.
Carries the immediate sequence into harmful alliances and their consequence.
Introduces repentance as an available reversal within the same immediate sequence.
Shows a clear prohibition redirecting allegiance toward submission.
Contrasts failure to act with acting on admonition, but lacks a mutual-restraint setting.
Shows a community trying to silence the one who rejects its wrongdoing.
A parallel threat turns demanded silence into coercive exclusion.
Establishes a communal body whose task includes restraining wrong.
Immediate doctrinal clarification, but it does not develop the restraint failure.
Makes wrong public and structural by joining obstruction and indecency in the assembly.
Generic observation of what people do.
An endpoint statement unrelated to mutual restraint.
Distinguishes those saved by publicly restraining evil from the punished wrongdoers.
Another positive communal profile of enjoining good and restraining wrong.
Immediate theological correction only.
Supplies a broad normative frame: justice and beneficence against indecency, wrong, and aggression.
Depicts grievous wrongdoing and deception but no act of restraint.
Completes the immediate sequence by connecting failed allegiance to persistent defiance.
Shows the consequence of arrogant persistence in what had been prohibited.
Hostile deceptive speech is present, but no communal prevention is developed.
Rescue follows the threatened messenger's episode without adding a restraint account.
Shows a settled social prohibition used to police exclusion, a contrary use of restraint.
Reasserts the public community's mandate to enjoin good and restrain wrong.
Offers an immediate contrast in religious leadership: humility rather than the prior failure of restraint.
Presents the inverse social order: enjoining wrong and forbidding good together.
No specific relation to restraint or shared wrongdoing.
Personal rejection of wrongdoing without an act of prevention.
Limits a prohibition in a different social setting; only a remote boundary parallel.
Guidance test unrelated to moral restraint.
Immediate receptive contrast, but it does not address preventing wrong.
Identifies false speech itself as munkar, extending the possible object of condemnation.
Generic recompense for deeds.
Battle perception and outcome do not illuminate mutual restraint.
Endpoint language only.
Divine accountability statement without a shared restraint relation.
Immediate faithful response, but no prevention of wrongdoing.
Shows prohibition turned against worship, a contrary misuse of stopping power.
Witnessing harm does not itself establish mutual restraint.
Generic consequence for deeds, without a preventive relation.
Boundary imagery is too remote from the focus's social practice.
Truth overturning false works gives only a general contrast with wrongdoing.
Immediate reward outcome, without developing the failure to restrain.
Presents self-restraint from desire as an individual counterpart to communal restraint.
Past deeds and accountability only.
Punishment context without a restraint relation.
Presents prophetic guidance as enjoining good, forbidding wrong, and restoring sound boundaries.
Obedient action under command is not a mutual-restraint parallel.
Immediate final consequence, but no added account of prevention.
Shows a prohibition deceptively recast, clarifying pressure against a protective boundary.
Connects return to previously prohibited conduct with persistence in falsehood.
Direct historical parallel: a surviving minority restrains corruption while the rest pursue corrupt ease.
Contrasts genuinely ending a course with returning to it, clarifying cessation and recurrence.
Combines blocking the divine way with bad conduct, a related contrary obstruction.
A timed legal notice without a relevant prevention relation.
Shows repeated return to prohibited, sinful private conduct after restraint has been imposed.
Adds guarding divine limits to the familiar public practice of restraining wrong.
Fear alone does not specify restraint of wrongdoing.
Generic precedent of rejection and punishment.
Action language is incidental to an unrelated episode.
Pairs receiving authorized guidance with stopping at a prohibition in an economic-social order.
Knowledge of deeds only.
Shows corrupt exchange leading to obstruction of the divine way and bad conduct.
Provides the setting of the Sabbath transgression behind the later restraint and punishment cards.
Depicts wrongful obstruction of sacred access, a contrary use of preventing power.
Places enjoining good and restraining wrong among responsibilities of established authority.
No specific relation to mutual restraint or the focus's wrong.
No relevant moral-prevention relation.
An isolated past deed without shared restraint.
Generic distinction of culpable groups and punishment.
Acceptance of good deeds and overlooking faults offer only a distant outcome contrast.
Unrelated tail-audit card.
Regret and professed reversal do not establish a restraint practice.
Worship and charitable practice are only a remote positive background.
Final inability to benefit or harm others is unrelated.
An individual conduct boundary, without the focus's mutual social dimension.
Repentance is a distant reversal motif rather than a prevention parallel.
Belated desire for righteous action lacks communal restraint.
Unrelated tail-audit card.
Unrelated creation argument.
Exclusion from a campaign is not a moral-prevention parallel.
Forbids unjust consumption and corrupt use of authority, closely complementing the corrupt gain in the 5:62-63 context.
Forbids obstructing a lawful reconciliation, preserving the distinction between rightful and wrongful restraint.
Makes preventing corruption through one group acting against another a condition for social preservation.
Pairs wrongdoing with remembrance, forgiveness, and refusal to persist, supplying an individual reversal of continued evil.
Privileges private speech that enjoins charity, recognized good, or reconciliation as socially corrective discourse.
Forbids collective cooperation in sin and aggression, a direct counterpart to shared tolerance of wrong.
Marks wrongful prohibition of permitted good as a boundary case against indiscriminate restraint.
Insists that the abundance of evil does not alter its moral distinction from good.
Provides a necessary boundary reading about personal guidance amid others' deviation; it does not erase the focus's communal critique.
Requires withdrawal from wrongful discourse until it changes, a nonparticipation response to public wrong.
Limits hostile speech to prevent reciprocal transgression, a narrower preventive boundary.
Specifies indecencies, sin, aggression, and false claims among the divinely prohibited wrongs.
Directly stages the question of why a community continues admonition before an anticipated judgment.
Combines enjoining recognized good with turning away from ignorant provocation.
Assigns a group the task of returning with warning, a communal preventive function.
Frames good deeds as removing bad deeds, an individual and communal repair motif.
Links a community's preservation to the presence of people actively engaged in reform.
Presents repelling evil with good as a constructive response rather than passive tolerance.
Supplies a wisdom-and-best-argument mode for corrective address.
A general prohibition of sexual wrongdoing without the focus's reciprocal social dimension.
Couples permitted provision with a prohibition against transgression and its consequence.
Identifies Satanic prompting as commanding indecency and munkar, directly naming the contrary moral direction.
Shows dignified nonparticipation in vain discourse, a limited social response.
Again presents repelling evil with good, reinforcing a non-retaliatory corrective pattern.
Commends avoidance of false allegiances and turning back to God, an individual boundary counterpart.
Makes responding to evil with what is better a transformative social corrective.
Joins avoidance of grave sins and indecencies with restraint in anger and forgiveness.
Keeps redress, pardon, and reconciliation in tension after wrongdoing rather than selecting one response.
Requires verification before acting on a report so that a group does not wrong others through ignorance.
Portrays collective intervention against aggression until return to the divine command, with justice after return.
Forbids private consultation in sin, aggression, and disobedience, directly complementing 58:8's repeated violation.
Treats harmful secret counsel as an injurious social tactic, clarifying the setting around 58:8-9.
Rebukes the gap between professed speech and action, a concise parallel to performative moral failure.
Intensifies the condemnation of saying what one does not do.
Places protective responsibility within households, extending prevention beyond the public setting.
Includes mutual urging toward truth and patience, a broad but less specific reciprocal ethic.
Challenges those who urge righteousness while neglecting their own conduct, sharpening the speech-action dimension.
Depicts a person who actively spreads corruption and destroys communal goods, naming a grave object of prevention.
Requires steadfast witness for justice even against oneself and close relations, supporting accountable moral intervention.
Prevents enmity from becoming injustice, a safeguard for corrective action.
Forbids corruption after rectification, supplying a direct anti-corruption norm.
Commands reform and forbids following the path of corrupters.
Warns of a collective trial that does not strike wrongdoers alone, directly supporting shared responsibility for public wrong.
Couples fair dealing with a warning against diminishing others and spreading corruption.
Defines the messenger's aim as reform to the extent possible, an active counterpart to passive tolerance.
Places change in a people's own condition, connecting collective moral agency with consequence.
Commands steadfast association with those who call on their Lord rather than following heedless desire.
Forbids obedience to excessive transgressors who spread corruption and do not reform.
Completes the depiction of those corrupters as agents of harm rather than reform.
Forbids harming others' due and moving through the land as corrupters.
Forbids seeking corruption while commanding beneficence from what one has received.
Connects manifest corruption in land and sea with what people have earned and consequential exposure to their deeds.
Condemns unjust harm to believing men and women, a concrete social wrong requiring protection.
Preserves a lone believer's warning against unjustly killing a messenger, modeling intervention within a coercive group.
Forbids social contempt, insult, and defamatory labeling, specifying communal wrongs that must not be normalized.
Links revealed measure and balance with people upholding justice, a wider institutional counterpart to restraining wrong.
